title: [v0.5.2] Contracts: define cross-component compatibility
author: mcpdev80
body:
## Goal

Make BaseHarbor's public compatibility boundaries explicit so CLI, stored state, capability providers and machine interfaces can evolve independently without contaminating portable application semantics.

> **Developer experience first.**
>
> **Stable contracts, minimal ceremony.**

## Compatibility boundaries

Document and verify at least:

```text
CLI/Core              <-> Portable Application Contract
CLI/Core              <-> Stored BaseHarbor State
Core                  <-> Capability Provider Protocol
CLI / JSON / MCP      <-> Shared Machine Result/Error Contract
Core                  <-> Runtime Provider Boundary
```

The public compatibility boundary is the documented specification/protocol, not internal Go package layout.

## Runtime and cloud neutrality

This release must preserve the ability to add later runtimes/platforms without rewriting application intent:

- Compose;
- Kubernetes;
- OpenShift;
- future AWS runtimes/services;
- future Azure runtimes/services;
- future GCP runtimes/services.

Hard rules:

- capability provider != runtime provider;
- cloud vendor != application intent;
- runtime implementation detail != portable application intent;
- managed cloud services remain replaceable capability/provider realizations.

No portable contract field may be added for Kubernetes/OpenShift/AWS/Azure/GCP merely because a future implementation may need it.

## Scope

- compatibility matrix for supported contract/protocol versions;
- capability-provider protocol compatibility guarantees;
- machine result/error compatibility guarantees;
- runtime-boundary compatibility rules;
- additive vs breaking evolution rules across those boundaries;
- clear unsupported-version diagnostics;
- tests proving supported combinations.

## Developer experience

- compatibility should be automatic in the normal path;
- errors identify the incompatible boundary and supported versions;
- do not expose internal version negotiations unless users need to act;
- do not freeze internal Go APIs unnecessarily;
- avoid adapters/shims until a demonstrated compatibility case requires them.

## Explicitly out of scope

- implementing Kubernetes/OpenShift/cloud runtimes;
- HA/topology semantics;
- provider catalog expansion;
- Go package ABI stability;
- enterprise identity/governance.

## Deployment/runtime compatibility boundary

The runtime-provider compatibility contract must be explicit enough for a restricted future runtime such as Kubernetes.

Add these compatibility boundaries:

```text
Deployment/Operator State <-> Runtime Provider
Runtime Access Reference  <-> Runtime Provider
Platform Resource Ref     <-> Runtime Provider
Runtime Capability Result <-> Shared Plan/Status/Error Model
```

### Deployment target compatibility

The Target contract itself comes from **#408 / v0.4.15**. This issue does not add Target/Context/Access/Scope semantics; it defines compatibility between that existing contract and Runtime Provider versions/components.

The public boundary must support:

- selecting a runtime;
- selecting a deployment target;
- associating an environment/deployment identity;
- providing runtime access by reference;
- referencing platform-owned resources;
- distinguishing BaseHarbor-owned vs platform/external resources.

It must not require runtime-specific portable fields.

### Runtime access semantics

A Runtime Provider may need authentication/authorization material, but the compatibility boundary exposes only a secret-safe reference/source abstraction.

The runtime implementation resolves that source.

Examples such as kubeconfig, OIDC or cloud auth are future implementations, not application-contract types.

### Restricted-permission runtimes

The Runtime Provider boundary must allow a provider to report:

- operation supported;
- operation unsupported;
- operation not authorized;
- guarantee unverifiable;
- ownership conflict;
- foreign ownership;
- degraded capability.

The shared core must be able to keep unrelated lifecycle operations available when only one feature is unavailable.

### Platform-owned resources

The Runtime Provider must be able to consume externally/platform-owned resources by deployment/operator reference without importing platform-specific identifiers into portable application intent.


## Capability semantic compatibility boundary

The compatibility model must distinguish three separate checks:

1. Capability Specification/version compatibility.
2. Application-required capability semantic-subset compatibility.
3. Availability/durability/topology guarantee compatibility.

The Capability Provider boundary must provide enough versioned metadata/results for the core to determine whether the provider satisfies the required semantic subset without exposing provider-specific product configuration in portable application intent.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Provider negotiation cannot silently treat partial semantic compatibility as full support.

- [ ] Cross-component compatibility documents capability-version, capability-semantic and availability-guarantee compatibility as separate concerns.

- [ ] Runtime providers can return permission/capability-aware typed outcomes without collapsing unrelated lifecycle operations.

- [ ] Platform-owned resource references are supported without runtime-specific portable fields.

- [ ] Runtime access is modeled as a secret-safe deployment reference/source rather than portable credentials.

- [ ] Deployment/operator-to-runtime compatibility is documented as a public boundary.

- [ ] Supported compatibility boundaries are documented and versioned.
- [ ] Capability providers can target the public protocol without BaseHarbor Core changes.
- [ ] CLI/JSON/MCP share compatible semantic result/error contracts.
- [ ] Runtime provider compatibility does not require portable-contract runtime fields.
- [ ] Architecture review confirms AWS/Azure/GCP can later supply runtimes and/or managed capability providers independently.
- [ ] Unsupported versions fail with actionable diagnostics.
- [ ] Compatibility tests cover supported and intentionally unsupported combinations.
- [ ] Internal implementation packages are not accidentally declared public compatibility surfaces.
- [ ] Validation follows `docs/DEVELOPMENT_GUIDELINES.md` economically.

Depends on: #175, #297
Parent roadmap: #155


## Delivery compatibility boundary

Cross-component compatibility must include Delivery Providers as a third independent provider axis.

Compatibility must distinguish:

1. Runtime Provider compatibility.
2. Capability Provider compatibility.
3. Delivery Provider compatibility.
4. Application-required capability semantic compatibility.
5. Portable availability/guarantee compatibility.

A compatible Delivery Provider must preserve BaseHarbor ownership, policy, verification and machine-result semantics regardless of whether it uses direct APIs, GitOps or another mechanism internally.


## Pre-release gate

Before creating this release:

- [ ] All acceptance criteria in this issue are complete.
- [ ] Required local/repository tests pass.
- [ ] The full relevant CI matrix has passed at least once on the **exact release-candidate commit**.
- [ ] Docker and Podman acceptance pass where applicable.
- [ ] Security, isolation and secret-leak checks pass where applicable.
- [ ] The documentation audit defined by #364 passes.
- [ ] Human-facing documentation matches the shipped behavior.
- [ ] Reference and normative specs match every changed public contract.
- [ ] No unresolved release blocker remains.
- [ ] Version, changelog, release notes and release metadata are consistent.
- [ ] Final exact-head acceptance evidence is recorded before tagging/releasing.

Acceptance answers whether the feature/release scope is complete. This gate answers whether the exact commit is safe and documented well enough to release.

Do not weaken or skip a required check merely to complete the release. Checks that are genuinely not applicable should be recorded as such rather than silently omitted.


## Provider Catalog compatibility boundary

Cross-component compatibility includes the catalog/distribution boundary but does not make catalog implementation details part of portable application semantics.

Add these public compatibility boundaries:

```text
Core <-> Provider Catalog Descriptor
Provider Catalog Descriptor <-> OCI Artifact Identity
Core <-> Provider Protocol
Core <-> Runtime Provider
Core <-> Capability Provider
Core <-> Delivery Provider
```

Compatibility must distinguish:

1. catalog descriptor schema/version compatibility;
2. provider implementation version compatibility;
3. Provider Protocol version compatibility;
4. service/capability contract version compatibility;
5. provider-family compatibility (runtime/capability/delivery);
6. OCI artifact identity/digest consistency.

A catalog match alone is never proof that a provider is usable. Resolution must still validate the relevant protocol, contract, semantic capability and platform requirements before mutation.

The existing "provider catalog expansion" out-of-scope rule means ecosystem breadth/public marketplace work remains deferred. The minimal Provider Catalog contract and compatibility rules required by the v0.5 freeze are in scope.

### Provider catalog compatibility acceptance

- [ ] Runtime, Capability and Delivery Provider descriptors use one versioned catalog contract with family-specific semantics.
- [ ] Unsupported descriptor/protocol/contract versions fail with an actionable compatibility error before mutation.
- [ ] Catalog resolution verifies OCI artifact identity/digest where an artifact is selected.
- [ ] Catalog metadata cannot bypass Provider Protocol or capability-semantic compatibility checks.
- [ ] Provider Catalog compatibility and Provider Runtime Registry state compatibility are tested as separate boundaries.


## Runtime-provider compatibility boundary

Cross-component compatibility must include the runtime-provider boundary established by #396.

Compatibility must keep these axes distinct:

1. BaseHarbor Core version;
2. Runtime Provider contract/protocol version;
3. Runtime Provider implementation version;
4. adopted standard/spec compatibility where relevant;
5. concrete runtime product/engine version;
6. OCI artifact digest/identity for externally distributed providers.

A runtime provider is compatible only when its contract/protocol version, declared semantic capabilities, required standards compatibility and target platform requirements satisfy the resolved deployment plan.

Product-version equality alone is not compatibility.

comments.body:
## Scope clarification: compatibility includes application-facing realization

#298 owns the formal compatibility relationships between the frozen components.

In addition to the existing boundaries, explicitly cover:

```
CLI/Core <-> BaseHarbor runtime image/API
Core     <-> capability/provider implementation version
Core     <-> persisted artifact/convergence state
Application capability contract <-> selected provider semantic support
```

Important distinction:

- application intent describes a logical capability (for example SQL);
- PostgreSQL is the current/default SQL provider realization;
- a future developer/operator may select another compatible provider;
- provider/product/version/digest remain visible facts but do not become portable application intent.

Compatibility reporting must tell a developer what matters to the application: contract/API/provider-version changes, deprecations and whether adaptation may be required. Detailed image/digest negotiation belongs in verbose/machine diagnostics.

Stale or incompatible artifacts must never be treated as compatible merely because a container/process is running.

## Standards-first compatibility axes

Cross-component compatibility must include the #391 boundaries:

1. BaseHarbor service-contract version.
2. Provider protocol version.
3. Provider implementation version.
4. Product/engine version.
5. Artifact digest/identity.
6. Standard protocol compatibility where applicable (for example RESP, S3 API, OTLP, OIDC).

These axes are independent. Compatibility must not infer service compatibility only from product name or container liveness.

Service Binding 1.1 output compatibility and JSON Schema 2020-12 schema compatibility belong in the compatibility matrix.
